title: Intracranial hemorrhage by layer
claims: Layers from outside in: scalp, skull, dura mater, arachnoid mater, subarachnoid space (CSF), pia mater, brain.
Epidural hematoma: blood between the skull and the dura, classically arterial from the middle meningeal artery torn by a temporal bone fracture near the pterion.
Epidural hematoma is biconvex (lens-shaped) on CT and does not cross suture lines, where the dura is firmly attached to the skull.
Epidural hematoma classically causes brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, then rapid deterioration from mass effect and herniation; treat with urgent surgical evacuation.
Subdural hematoma: blood between the dura and the arachnoid, usually venous from torn bridging veins that cross from the cortex to the dural venous sinuses.
Subdural hematoma is crescent-shaped on CT and crosses suture lines, but does not cross the falx or tentorium.
Subdural hematoma risk factors: older age (brain atrophy stretches bridging veins), alcohol use, anticoagulation, and abusive head trauma in infants.
Subarachnoid hemorrhage: blood between the arachnoid and the pia, in the CSF of the sulci, fissures and basal cisterns.
Most non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage comes from a ruptured berry aneurysm: thunderclap 'worst headache of my life' and neck stiffness.
Suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage: non-contrast head CT first; if negative, lumbar puncture for xanthochromia. Complications include vasospasm (nimodipine) and hydrocephalus.
sources: StatPearls: Acute Stroke: Evaluation and Management. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535369/
